title: Don't Move
full_review:
"Don't Move" (Northern Arts) was a hit when it was released in Italy as "Non Ti Muovere" in early 2004, which must say something about the European penchant for soggy, angst-filled romance.

The film is a heavy-breathing potboiler about a doctor, Timoteo (Sergio Castellitto), who has just learned that his daughter's been in a near-fatal motorcycle accident.

As he sits in shock outside the operating room, he reminisces about a time 16 years earlier when his car broke down and he raped Italia, the young impoverished woman who let him use her phone. (This is Penelope Cruz in an admirably intense, no-holds-barred performance.) Back home, he's wracked with guilt, and later goes back to see Italia again. Does she reject him? Not a bit. Starved for love herself, and -- we later learn -- abused as a child by her father, she enters into an obsessively passionate and kinky relationship with him. (The sex scenes are brief but graphic, though there's little nudity.)

Timoteo's bourgeois wife, Elsa (Claudia Gerini), seems to intuit the adulterous affair but remains silent. Just as Timoteo is about to confess all to Elsa, the latter informs him she's pregnant.

Castellitto himself directed this alternately sentimental and repellant adaptation of wife Margaret Mazzantini's best seller. The reasonably high-caliber acting and artsy trappings can't erase the considerable sordidness of the plot even with its tacked-on "redemptive" ending. (Midway through the film, Timoteo informs Italia he doesn't believe God exists. Later, he changes his mind. Big deal.) For all his soul-searching, he remains self-pityingly unsympathetic.

Our advice: Don't go.

In Italian. Subtitles.

The film contains much rough and crude language, brutal sexual encounters, abortion, partial nudity, graphic operating room gore, and gratuitous scenes of bodily functions. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. Not rated by the Motion Picture Association of America.
